To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) an N‐terminal fragment of mutant huntingtin accumulates in postsynaptic densities in the brains of R 6/2 mice, 2) a similar fragment of wild‐type huntingin is present in the human brain and 3) both mutant and wild type fragments bind to synaptic membranes and perturb the membrane bilayer, which may be an early step in the pathogenesis of Huntington's disease.
